title: Palaces of pearls
hookLine: if I had palaces of pearls and jewels, may I never forget You (Sri Rag M1, ang 14)

lines: A REAL ESTATE APP AT MIDNIGHT.
GURU NANAK BUILDS A DREAM HOUSE.
cards: A real estate app, late at night. Infinity pool. Floor-to-ceiling windows over the ocean.
A kitchen bigger than a whole apartment, a garden, room for everyone you love. Guru Nanak built a dream house too, in words.
Near the start of the Guru Granth Sahib's main body, in Sri Rag, he raises a palace wall by jeweled wall. And then he asks one question about it.

teach.h: A PALACE OF PEARLS AND MUSK.
teach.b: The shabad is on ang 14. It begins, in effect: if I had a palace built of pearls, inlaid with jewels, its walls plastered with musk and saffron, sandalwood and aloe, a joy to come home to.
Then the turn: let it not be that, seeing all this, I go astray, forget You, and Your Name no longer comes to mind.
Then the refrain, the rahao, the line tradition treats as the hymn's center: without the Lord my soul burns to ashes; I asked my Guru, and I saw there is no other place.
Then he does it again, three more times, each bigger. If the floor were paved with diamonds and rubies, and a beautiful companion waited on a jeweled bed.

If I became a siddha, a yogi with miraculous powers, appearing and vanishing at will. If I became a sultan, raising armies, sitting on a throne, giving orders. Each time, the same ending: let me not forget You.
Notice what Guru Nanak doesn't say.
He doesn't say palaces are evil, or beauty is a trap, or the rich are lost. Sikh teaching doesn't ask people to give up homes, families or work; the Gurus lived as householders.
The danger he names is narrower and sharper: forgetting. A beautiful thing can fill the view so completely that the Giver drops out of the picture.
The hymn doesn't ask for less. It asks to remember, even with more. And it's set in Sri Rag, a raag tradition associates with evening and seriousness: a grave melody for a dream house.

how: Sikhs sing this Sri Rag shabad of Guru Nanak in kirtan; its refrain, that without the Lord the soul burns and there is no other place, is often the line congregations repeat.

o: the refrain, the hymn's center line
the first line that names the raag

games.q: palaces of pearls — tap the pairs.
p: built of pearls, inlaid with jewels
without the Lord, my soul burns

s: the hymn says palaces and beauty are evil
the danger it names is forgetting the Giver, not the gift.
the same ending returns four times
each bigger picture ends: let me not forget You.
Sikh teaching asks people to give up homes and families
the Gurus lived as householders; the hymn asks to remember, even with more.

games.q: you're offered a palace of pearls, walls of musk and sandalwood. what does Guru Nanak ask for?
o: that it not make him forget You.
games.why: he neither grabs nor refuses. he asks to keep remembering the One even with everything.

practice: Build your dream house in your mind, the view, the kitchen, the morning light, whoever you'd want there, and enjoy it for a few breaths; you're allowed.
Then ask Guru Nanak's question: in that house, would I still remember what matters most, still call my mother, still notice the person who cleans the pool?
Let the house go gently, like setting down a heavy box, and if you pray, say Waheguru as you let go.

wordCard.voice: Rahao, the refrain, the line tradition treats as a hymn's center: here, after every luxury and power Guru Nanak imagines, it asks only this, that none of it make him forget the One.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: pearl; the hymn opens with a palace built of pearls.

carryVoice: Your line: may I not forget. Not less, just remembering. Day six hundred forty-seven, done.

sources.ref: Sri Rag M1, Ang 14 (moti ta mandar oosareh)
